newsitem.title: USA: US chip industry book-to-bill fell to 1.10 in Dec.
newsitem.headline: US chip industry book-to-bill fell to 1.10 in Dec.

text.p: The U.S. semiconductor industry's key indicator fell in December, reflecting softening orders despite strong sales.

The U.S. Semiconductor Industry Association said Thursday the December book-to-bill ratio, which measures the dollar value of orders against sales the industry shipped in the month, fell to 1.10 from a revised 1.16 ratio in November.
But 1.10 is still a strong number, meaning orders topped sales volume. The ratio means manufactures received $110 in new orders last month for every $100 worth of chips they sold.
Industry analysts had expected the ratio to be about flat with the November figure.

The ratio, a leading indicator of future demand tallied by the industry's trade group, has been improving recently, reflecting an increase in orders by personal computer makers and more stable prices for memory chip prices.
The SIA said December's book-to-bill ratio fell from November's because sales rose at the same time as orders fell, sharpening the contrast between the two sides of the ratio.
Sales rose 2.7 percent for American semiconductor makers to $3.52 billion from November's $3.43 billion, it said.
However, orders fell 2.9 percent in December to $3.87 billion from $3.98 billion in November.
The organization revised its book-to-bill figure for November to 1.16 from a preliminary 1.15 reported last month.
"We remain optimistic about prospects for growth in 1997," SIA president Thomas W. Armstrong said in a statement.

Compared with a year earlier, both bookings and sales were lower in December from the same month in 1995. December bookings fell 22.8 percent from the year earlier month, while December sales or billings fell 21.2 percent from December of 1995, which was a record high.
The SIA said that, globally in 1996, semiconductor chip revenues fell 10 percent to about $130 billion.
The December report is the last the SIA will issue describing a book-to-bill ratio for the American market.
The organization is replacing the report with a one on global sales with a breakdown of industry sales in each of four regions.

But the new report will have no bookings or orders data -- which is the information Wall Street analysts say is the most useful in the report. Though the book to bill was often criticized, it was widely watched.
The SIA has said that a report on the American market only has lost its usefulness because most semiconductor manufacturers sell their goods globally.

Analysts have complained that the formula the SIA has used to compile the book-to-bill ratio, which adjusts the figures for seasonality and weighs them for a three month moving average, often distorts the real order picture.
But the absense of an industry-wide book-to-bill figure might add more volatility to semiconductor stocks, said Charles Boucher of UBS Securities and Nimal Vallipuram of Bear Stearns & Co.
